As modern software development accelerates through automated scaffolding and AI code generation, functional applications can be spun up faster than ever. However, this velocity often introduces a recurring aesthetic dilemma: products that execute their intended features smoothly yet look visually indistinct, bland, or unfinished. Maker HYEON GYE YONG launched Polishory on Product Hunt specifically to address this gap. The platform targets the ambiguous instruction to "make it look better," translating vague design dissatisfaction into structured, tactical evaluations. Rather than making assertions about whether artificial intelligence generated a site, Polishory provides a measurable design guide aimed at helping builders eliminate visual clutter and prevent what the tech community increasingly terms "AI slop."

The developer intends to expand Polishory beyond the initial challenge, focusing on improving recommendation accuracy and delivering even clearer execution steps for developers.

Discover how solo founder Rishi Mohan scaled Orshot to $6.2K MRR and 760k+ visual renders through building in public and SEO.
...
Rishi has worked as a designer and front-end engineer for almost ten years, at places like Instahyre, BigBinary and Borg. The whole time he was quietly building his own things on the side. Eventually one of them worked, and he went all in on building for himself.
...
### Building in Public
...
A big part of how I even got here is building in public on X.
...
I've been sharing what I make over at @thelifeofrishi for years, posting revenue numbers, features, wins and failures, and that habit changed my life more than once. It's honestly what got me my job in Berlin and my move from India in the first place, because people in the startup world already knew my work from X. The same audience is what later gave Pika its first users, and then Orshot.
...
I started building Orshot in February 2025. Around that time, it felt like a nudge to go full on building my own stuff without the cushion of a full-time job. So I put everything into Orshot, registered DaSkrad and launched it the same month.
...
The thing that helped me a lot in the beginning was that I wasn't really starting from scratch. I'd already spent a few years building Pika, my screenshots and mockups tool, which had crossed $100k in earnings just from SEO, building in public (examples below) and word of mouth.
...
So when Orshot went live, a lot of those same people, mostly developers and indie makers who already followed me from years of building in public, were the first ones to try it. A good chunk of my initial customers came from the Pika crowd.
...
I write long comparison posts (the most converting and highest traffic intent), how-to guides and tool roundups that slowly climb the rankings and keep bringing in people who are actively looking for something like Orshot.
...
I used to think a strong Product Hunt launch or a viral post would be the thing that changed everything, but for me those never really moved the needle in a lasting way. The spikes come and go in a day.
...
What actually built this was patient, unglamorous SEO, showing up consistently while building in public, and slowly earning a bit of a reputation, so that's where I put my energy now.
...
Right now Orshot is still just me, doing around 5,000 users, about $6.2K MRR and 760k+ renders so far. I keep all the numbers public on orshot.com/open.

Yes — Tony operates TypingMind, DevUtils, and Xnapper as a solo developer from Vietnam. He's been public about this in his newsletter (news.tonydinh.com) and Indie Hackers posts. Two factors: he sold Black Magic for $128K when the unit economics broke, which gave him runway, and he had already been posting publicly on Indie Hackers and X for years, which meant he had audience credibility when he launched TypingMind. Solo founders who build on a single platform without either (a) an exit option or (b) an independent distribution channel are in a much more fragile position. Tony had both. Anyone building on a single LLM provider API today is taking a similar bet — worth internalizing that the platform's pricing can change and plan accordingly.

Partially. The TypingMind / DevUtils pattern — niche interface products for technical buyers — does require building or commissioning the software, which is harder without code skills. However, the distribution playbook (build in public, publish revenue, ship fast, iterate on buyer feedback) is entirely replicable regardless of technical depth. And with AI coding tools (Cursor, Claude Code, Tycoon's AI CTO) a 'non-technical' founder can now prototype and ship products that would have required hiring engineers five years ago. The gap is narrowing each year.

...
A bootstrapped AI logo tool that hit $8.4k in four months through a Product Hunt launch and a relentless SEO and backlink grind.
...
Berk Elmas is a software engineer who moved from roles at startups and larger companies into building his own products. With co-founders Burak Uyar and Can Elbirlik, he started Sketch Logo AI around the start of 2024. The premise was simple: most AI logo tools rely only on text prompts, so they set out to let people sketch a rough idea and have the model finish it into a usable logo, 3D visual, or illustration. The pitch they kept repeating was that you sketch, the AI completes it, and no design background is needed.
...
The first big push came from Product Hunt. The launch landed at number five product of the day in January, and the first paying customer arrived within roughly 72 hours. That early signal mattered, but Berk has been clear that the real engine was search. He treated SEO as a priority from day one, bought a SaaS boilerplate that came with a marketing guide and a list of over 150 directories to chase backlinks, and published steadily, close to 29 blog posts in six months alongside regular social posts.
...
The compounding worked. By his own account the tool cleared about $8.4k in revenue inside the first four months, the milestone he shared in his Reddit post, and it kept climbing toward $25k by the six month mark. One strong week brought in around $2.9k, driven largely by content and backlinks rather than paid ads, and traffic at points reached well into the hundreds of thousands of monthly views. It was bootstrapped throughout, with no outside funding and no paid acquisition.

Kostya Nesterovich's Seline Analytics reached $1K MRR after 16 months, despite a domain migration that knocked the homepage out of Google for exactly six months.
...
Seline Analytics did not reach $1K MRR in a straight line. Kostya Nesterovich built it as a simple, privacy-friendly alternative to Google Analytics, but a domain move from .so to .com created a brutal growth stall. For exactly six months, even the homepage disappeared from Google search.

...
In January 2026, Seline crossed $1,000 MRR after 16 months. Kostya's reflection was not a victory lap about revenue screenshots; it was a reminder that growth comes from unpredictable places. A small Reddit comment can start a customer relationship, a modest X post can reach someone tracking millions of events, and a minor feature can be the final reason someone signs up. At $1K MRR, Seline's bottleneck had shifted from product to distribution.
...
The median of the 294 documented journeys with this milestone is 6 months; this one took 16 months.
...
Kostya built Seline because no existing simple analytics tool covered both website and in-app SaaS analytics the way he and his team wanted to use themselves.
...
No landing page, waitlist or survey step is described. The founder picked the idea against a personal checklist (existing validated competitors, organic search demand, personal daily use, B2B) and then built straight to a usable v1.

Reaching a usable first version took about six months of iteration before any public launch.
...

Migrating the product's domain from seline.so to seline.com wiped the site, including the homepage, out of Google search entirely.
...
What they did instead: No specific fix is described; the founder says visibility and growth resumed on their own once the six-month window passed, while he kept shipping product (faster dashboards, an AI chat feature, a public API, WordPress and Framer integrations) instead of pausing.
...
At $1K MRR the founder frames the bottleneck as distribution, not product: of roughly 74,000 homepage visitors to date, only a small slice are the right audience.

"After Six Years of Development, Sunken Realms Descends onto Steam Today" - Games Press
...
### Press release 

18/09/20
...
September 18, 2026 | The wait is over. After 6 years in development, Magic Puncher Games' Sunken Realms, a focused ARPG dungeon crawler with rogue-lite elements, is out now on Steam at $16.99 / £13.99 / €16.99, with a 10% launch discount for the first two weeks. The gates of Aedaria are open, with 45,000 wishlists already logged and adventurers ready to descend. The demo remains live until September 21st for anyone who wants a first taste before diving into the full journey.
...
"The game that inspired me to make my own was Outward," said Brad Warren, the solo developer behind Magic Puncher Games. "It has such a feeling of adventure and the wide unknown that I haven't quite felt anywhere else. Sunken Realms went in its own direction over time, but I hope it kept that same spirit." That spirit carries through the game today, alongside the storytelling influence of Hades and the sense of adventure found in The Legend of Zelda.
...

...
About Magic Puncher Games Magic Puncher Games is a solo development studio helmed by Brad Warren, who has spent the last six years bringing Sunken Realms to life.
